extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (life-sciences/nature-based claims)
extracted.subtask_description: A worksheet to guide 35 U.S.C. §101 Subject Matter Eligibility (SME) analysis for claims directed to nature‑based products, walking an examiner through identifying the invention, establishing the BRI, Step 1 statutory-category, Step 2A exception/marked-difference, and Step 2B ‘significantly more’/inventive-concept considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify applicant's invention and establish BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim based on plain meaning and the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim. Example: for a vaccine claim, the BRI may be (i) a sufficient amount of Peptide F to produce an immunogenic response and (ii) a sufficient amount of carrier substances to make a carrier suitable for administration. Use plain-meaning analysis (e.g., what 'cream' means in the pharmaceutical arts) and identify embodiments encompassed by the BRI. If an examiner will assume an amendment to make a claim fall into a statutory category, make that assumption clear in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A or B. If 'No', make a rejection that the claim is drawn to non-statutory subject matter (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, consider continuing the SME analysis under that assumption and document it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — is the claim directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the claim is 'directed' to a product of nature, a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicially recognized exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature when it recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart. Abstract ideas include fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, or mathematical relationships/formulae. Use case law charts and the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance for assistance. Choose A (no), B (yes but streamlined analysis appropriate), or C (yes — proceed to marked-difference analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (nature-based products)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a nature-based product limitation, identify the limitation(s), identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart(s), and compare to determine whether the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics compared to the counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete parts (a) identify the limitation(s); (b) identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart(s) (e.g., components if the claimed mixture has no naturally occurring counterpart); (c) compare and choose (i) exhibits markedly different characteristics (eligible) or (ii) lacks markedly different characteristics (exception). Provide specific factual reasoning (e.g., changed form, physical properties, adherence, or changed functional property such as enhanced immunogenicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics considered for 'markedly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of characteristics the courts consider when determining marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype, including functional and structural characteristics; and structure and form, whether chemical, genetic, or physical. Use these factors when comparing the claimed limitation to its natural counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-claim exception for marked-difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Process claims are generally not subject to the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis for nature-based products, except in limited situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only apply the marked-difference analysis to a process claim when the process claim is drafted so there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple'). Otherwise, analyze product limitations only where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — additional elements / 'significantly more' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception by identifying any additional elements beyond the exception and evaluating their significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A. Are there additional elements beyond the exception? If 'No', conclude SME analysis with a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). If 'Yes', list the additional elements and continue. Note: where a product claim comprises a combination of components that do not occur together in nature, each component should be considered as an additional element to the other components when determining whether the combination results in significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / inventive concept considerations (reasons supporting significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate identified additional elements (individually and in combination) to determine whether they provide an 'inventive concept' such that the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions; not adding mere words 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well‑understood, routine and conventional in the field (do not append known routine activities at a high level); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations amounting to more than generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Use these factors and the provided anti‑patterns when drafting the examiner's reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a streamlined SME analysis when eligibility is self-evident and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply streamlined analysis when the claimed invention is not focused on an exception and 'clearly does not attempt to tie up an exception such that others cannot practice it' (refer to February 2015 Training Slides for examples). If appropriate, conclude SME analysis and continue with other examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and suggest disclosure elements that could render a claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Search the disclosure for elements that could be added to the claim that may make it eligible and consider suggesting them to applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples where possible (e.g., the disclosed element of an 'immuno-effective amount of an aluminum salt adjuvant' might make a vaccine claim eligible — see claim 5 of Example 28). Record suggested amendments in the file where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural guidance: use of form paragraphs and sample rejection language
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that a claim is ineligible, use specified form paragraphs and include clear sample rejection language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (and 7.05.01 as applicable) available in Custom OACs. The worksheet provides sample §101 rejection language describing why the claim is directed to a judicial exception and why additional elements do not amount to significantly more; customize factual details to the claim under review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude SME analysis and proceed to other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If any elements (individually or combined) amount to significantly more than the exception, conclude the SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the SME analysis finds eligibility, document reasoning and proceed with novelty, nonobviousness, enablement, etc. If ineligible, make the §101 rejection and continue with other examinations as required; clarify the record with remarks where helpful (for example, explain how a claim recites a product-of-nature 'x' but with additional element 'y' amounts to significantly more).
